Guideline: Rely on React Compiler where enabled; memoize by measurement otherwise
Description: React Compiler (1.0) memoizes components and values automatically at build time. For new code the docs recommend relying on it and using useMemo/useCallback as escape hatches, for example to stabilize an effect dependency; leave existing memoization in place unless you test its removal. Without the compiler, memoize computations that profiling shows are expensive.
Do: Check whether the compiler is enabled; add useMemo for measured hot paths or effect dependencies
Don't: Wrap every value in useMemo by default, or strip existing memoization without testing
Code Good: const visible = useMemo(() => filterRows(rows, query), [rows, query]); // measured hot path or effect dependency
Code Bad: const label = useMemo(() => `${first} ${last}`, [first, last]); // trivial work

Description: useCallback keeps a function identity stable for memoized children or effect dependencies. With React Compiler enabled this happens automatically; without it, use useCallback where a stable identity is actually consumed.
Do: useCallback for handlers passed to memoized children

Guideline: Read form values from FormData unless you need them while typing
Description: A form action receives FormData with every named input, so inputs can stay uncontrolled. Control an input with value and onChange only when the UI needs the value on every keystroke, such as live validation or a dependent field.
Do: Named uncontrolled inputs read through FormData; controlled inputs only where each keystroke matters
Don't: value/onChange state for every field just to submit it
Code Good: <form action={save}><input name="email" type="email" /></form> // save(formData) reads formData.get('email')
Code Bad: const [email, setEmail] = useState(''); <input value={email} onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} /> // only used on submit

Description: Starting in React 19 the form action prop is the preferred submission API: React passes FormData to the function, runs it in a Transition, manages pending state and resets uncontrolled fields after it succeeds. onSubmit with e.preventDefault() still works for manual handling. With a Server Function as the action, the form can submit before JavaScript loads.
Do: <form action={fn}>; requestFormReset when handling submission manually
Don't: onClick on the submit button as the only handler
Code Bad: <button type="button" onClick={handleSubmit}>Post</button> // not a form submission: no FormData, pending state or reset

Guideline: useActionState for action results and pending state
Description: useActionState(reducerAction, initialState) returns [state, dispatchAction, isPending]. Pass dispatchAction to the form action to show the last result, such as validation errors, and the pending flag; with a Server Function the action receives the previous state and FormData.
Don't: Hand-rolled loading and error state around a form action
Code Good:
const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(signup, undefined);
{state?.error &&

{state.error}

Code Bad: const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false); const [error, setError] = useState(null); async function onSubmit(e) { e.preventDefault(); setLoading(true); /* ... */ }

Description: useFormStatus returns the pending state of the parent <form>, so it must be called in a component rendered inside that form. It does not report on a form rendered in the same component.
Do: Call useFormStatus in a child component such as the submit button
Don't: Call useFormStatus in the component that renders the <form>
Code Good: function SubmitButton() { const { pending } = useFormStatus(); return <button disabled={pending}>Save</button>; } // rendered inside <form>
Code Bad: function Form() { const { pending } = useFormStatus(); return <form action={save}>...</form>; } // never reports this form

Guideline: Read promises and context with use
Description: use(resource) reads a Promise or a context during render and, unlike Hooks, can be called inside conditions and loops. A component reading a Promise suspends until it resolves, so wrap it in Suspense (and an Error Boundary for rejection). Promises must be cached so the same instance is reused across re-renders; a Promise created during render is not.
Do: Pass a cached or server-created Promise to use() under a Suspense boundary
Don't: Create a new Promise in render and pass it to use()
Code Good:
function Comments({ commentsPromise }) { const comments = use(commentsPromise); return comments.map((c) =>

{c.text}

Code Bad: function Comments({ id }) { const comments = use(fetch(`/api/comments/${id}`).then((r) => r.json())); } // new Promise every render

Guideline: ref is a regular prop in React 19
Description: Starting in React 19 function components receive ref as a prop, so new components do not need forwardRef; React plans to deprecate and remove forwardRef in a future version.
Do: Destructure ref from props and pass it to the element
Don't: Wrap new function components in forwardRef
Code Good: function TextField({ label, ref, ...props }) { return <label>{label}<input ref={ref} {...props} /></label>; }
Code Bad: const TextField = forwardRef(function TextField(props, ref) { ... }); // not needed in React 19
